chunks: And it was narrated from Al-ʿAlāʾ ibn Sayābah, who said:
I asked Abā ʿAbdillāh عليه السلام about the testimony of one who plays with pigeons. He said: “There is no harm, if he is not known for fisq.”

I said: Those around us say that ʿUmar said: he is a devil. So he said: “Glory be to Allah! Did you not know that the Messenger of Allah صلى الله عليه وآله said: ‘Indeed, the angels flee at wagering and curse its participant, except in the case of the hoof, the hoofed foot, the feather, and the arrowhead, for the angels attend them.’ And the Messenger of Allah صلى الله عليه وآله raced Usāmah ibn Zayd and set horses running.”

key_terms.الرِّيشَ: the feather; referring to birds in lawful competition
key_terms.النَّصْلَ: the arrowhead; referring to archery-related competition
key_terms.الْحَافِرَ: the hoof; a category of permitted competitive activity
key_terms.الْمَلَائِكَةَ: the angels, who withdraw from certain blameworthy acts
key_terms.بِالْحَمَامِ: with pigeons; referring to pigeon play or keeping them for play
key_terms.بِفِسْقٍ: with sinfulness; known open immoral conduct affecting probity
key_terms.شَهَادَةِ: legal testimony given in a judicial context

ai.seo_question: Is the testimony of someone who plays with pigeons accepted in Islamic law?
ai.summary: This hadith discusses the legal acceptability of the testimony of a person who plays with pigeons, stating that it is acceptable so long as he is not known for open sinfulness. It also distinguishes blameworthy wagering from permitted competitive activities associated with riding, birds, and weaponry, citing the practice and saying of the Messenger of Allah صلى الله عليه وآله.
